claim: Fluoroquinolones are the recommended antimicrobial treatment for typhoid.
source: Fluoroquinolones (FQ) are the recommended antimicrobial treatment for typhoid, a severe systemic infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established medical practice.

claim: Typhoid is a severe systemic infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
source: Fluoroquinolones (FQ) are the recommended antimicrobial treatment for typhoid, a severe systemic infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about the causative agent of typhoid.

claim: FQ-resistance mutations in S. Typhi have become common.
source: FQ-resistance mutations in S. Typhi have become common, hindering treatment and control efforts.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of antimicrobial resistance.

claim: FQ-resistance mutations hinder treatment and control efforts.
source: FQ-resistance mutations in S. Typhi have become common, hindering treatment and control efforts.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of resistance on public health.

claim: Six out of 11 mutants carried a selective advantage over the antimicrobial-sensitive parent strain in the absence of antimicrobial pressure.
source: In the absence of antimicrobial pressure, 6 out of 11 mutants carried a selective advantage over the antimicrobial-sensitive parent strain, indicating that FQ resistance in S. Typhi is not typically associated with fitness costs.
evidence: This is a direct result from the competition experiments performed in the study.

claim: FQ resistance in S. Typhi is not typically associated with fitness costs.
source: In the absence of antimicrobial pressure, 6 out of 11 mutants carried a selective advantage over the antimicrobial-sensitive parent strain, indicating that FQ resistance in S. Typhi is not typically associated with fitness costs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing positive selection coefficients.

claim: Double-mutants exhibited higher than expected fitness as a result of synergistic epistasis.
source: Double-mutants exhibited higher than expected fitness as a result of synergistic epistasis, signifying that epistasis may be a critical factor in the evolution and molecular epidemiology of S. Typhi.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of fitness coefficients for double mutants.

claim: Epistasis may be a critical factor in the evolution and molecular epidemiology of S. Typhi.
source: Double-mutants exhibited higher than expected fitness as a result of synergistic epistasis, signifying that epistasis may be a critical factor in the evolution and molecular epidemiology of S. Typhi.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the broader implications of the epistasis findings.

claim: FQ-resistant strains would be naturally maintained even if fluoroquinolone use were reduced.
source: Our findings have important implications for the management of drug-resistant S. Typhi, suggesting that FQ-resistant strains would be naturally maintained even if fluoroquinolone use were reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive fitness coefficients observed in the absence of antimicrobials.

claim: The evolution of antimicrobial resistance in bacteria is driven by the pressure of sustained exposure to antimicrobials.
source: The evolution of antimicrobial resistance in bacteria is driven by the pressure of sustained exposure to antimicrobials.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of antimicrobial resistance.

claim: Resistance to a specific antimicrobial typically confers a reduction in Darwinian fitness in the absence of the pressure induced by that antimicrobial.
source: This term is misleading in the sense that resistance to a specific antimicrobial typically confers a reduction in Darwinian fitness (a fitness cost) in the absence of the pressure induced by that antimicrobial (Andersson and Levin, 1999; Andersson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bacterial mutations that appear to have a low fitness cost or no fitness cost are sometimes observed.
source: Nevertheless, bacterial mutations that appear to have a low fitness cost or no fitness cost are sometimes observed, and mutations that may induce a fitness benefit in the absence of antimicrobials have been described but are rare (Macvanin et al., 2003; Enne et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2005; Kassen and Bataillon, 2006; Rozen et al., 2007; Marcusson et al., 2009; Bataillon et al., 2011; Miskinyte and Gordo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations that may induce a fitness benefit in the absence of antimicrobials have been described but are rare.
source: Nevertheless, bacterial mutations that appear to have a low fitness cost or no fitness cost are sometimes observed, and mutations that may induce a fitness benefit in the absence of antimicrobials have been described but are rare (Macvanin et al., 2003; Enne et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2005; Kassen and Bataillon, 2006; Rozen et al., 2007; Marcusson et al., 2009; Bataillon et al., 2011; Miskinyte and Gordo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Clinicians have become progressively reliant on the fluoroquinolones for treating infections caused by Enterobacteriacea over the past 20 years.
source: Over the past 20 years, as a consequence of resistance to multiple first-line antimicrobials in the Enterobacteriacea, clinicians have become progressively reliant on the fluoroquinolones for treating infections caused by this Gram-negative bacterial family (Parry, 2004; Vinh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Resistance to fluoroquinolones has become common within the Enterobacteriacea.
source: The increasing usage and dependency on the fluoroquinolones has coincided with resistance to fluoroquinolones becoming common within the Enterobacteriacea (Le et al., 2009; Butler, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Antimicrobial therapy is essential for treatment of typhoid.
source: This change is highly pertinent for diseases like typhoid, a severe invasive infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (Parry et al., 2002), as antimicrobial therapy is essential for treatment.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Typhoid remains common in many developing countries.
source: Typhoid remains common in many developing countries, and increasing minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, correlate with increased fever clearance times and treatment failure (Parry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Increasing minimum inhibitory concentrations to fluoroquinolones correlate with increased fever clearance times and treatment failure.
source: Typhoid remains common in many developing countries, and increasing minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, correlate with increased fever clearance times and treatment failure (Parry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Elevated MICs to fluoroquinolones observed in S. Typhi are a consequence of mutations in the DNA gyrase gene, gyrA, and secondary mutations in the topoisomerase gene, parC.
source: The elevated MICs to fluoroquinolones observed in S. Typhi are a consequence of mutations in the DNA gyrase gene, gyrA, and secondary mutations in the topoisomerase gene, parC (Chau et al., 2007; Parry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several different gyrA mutations have arisen independently in multiple lineages of S. Typhi.
source: Evidence of strong selection for these mutations can be observed within the phylogenetic structure of S. Typhi, as several different gyrA mutations have arisen independently in multiple lineages (Roumagnac et al., 2006; Holt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: Twelve individual S. Typhi mutants were constructed by introducing one or more single mutations into the gyrA and parC genes of a host S. Typhi strain by allelic exchange.
source: We constructed 12 individual S. Typhi mutants, seven of which have been isolated clinically, by introducing one or more single mutations into the gyrA and parC genes of a host S. Typhi strain by allelic exchange (Turner et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Seven of the constructed mutants have been isolated clinically.
source: We constructed 12 individual S. Typhi mutants, seven of which have been isolated clinically, by introducing one or more single mutations into the gyrA and parC genes of a host S. Typhi strain by allelic exchange (Turner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the mutants constructed.

claim: The seven mutants with naturally occurring equivalents all demonstrated significant increases in MICs over the parent strain with all tested antimicrobials.
source: The seven mutants with naturally occurring equivalents all demonstrated significant increases in MICs over the parent strain with all tested antimicrobials.
evidence: This is based on experimental MIC measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The increases in MICs were comparable to those observed in clinical isolates with the corresponding natural mutations.
source: The increases in MICs were comparable to those observed in clinical isolates with the corresponding natural mutations (Chau et al., 2007; Parry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited clinical data.

claim: Double mutants exhibited greater MICs than single mutants.
source: Double mutants exhibited greater MICs than single mutants and the triple mutant exhibited the highest MIC to all tested fluoroquinolones (Parry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on experimental MIC measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The triple mutant exhibited the highest MIC to all tested fluoroquinolones.
source: Double mutants exhibited greater MICs than single mutants and the triple mutant exhibited the highest MIC to all tested fluoroquinolones (Parry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on experimental MIC measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The control strain demonstrated no significant difference from the parent S. Typhi strain.
source: The four strains without a naturally occurring counterpart also demonstrated higher MICs than the parent strain, and the control strain—a strain containing a mutation in the defunct aroC gene—demonstrated no significant difference from the parent S. Typhi strain (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental MIC measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: Allele frequencies measured by bacterial enumeration and pyrosequencing demonstrated a strong linear relationship (r2 = 0.90).
source: Allele frequencies measured by bacterial enumeration and pyrosequencing demonstrated a strong linear relationship (r2 = 0.90, Figure 1)
evidence: This is based on experimental validation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Measurement by pyrosequencing exhibited less variation among replicates than classical culture and enumeration.
source: with measurement by pyrosequencing exhibiting less variation among replicates than classical culture and enumeration (p<4 × 10−4 for all nine starting dilutions between 0.1 and 0.9; 6.4 < F17,17 < 38.1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The pyrosequencing assay is an accurate and highly reproducible method for determining the specific allele frequencies in mixed bacterial suspensions over a range of concentrations.
source: These data indicate our pyrosequencing assay is an accurate and highly reproducible method for determining the specific allele frequencies in mixed bacterial suspensions over a range on concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation data.

claim: Selection coefficients for two mutants (D87N, S83Y) were not statistically different from zero.
source: Maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) of the selection coefficients of two mutants (D87N, S83Y) were not statistically different from zero (exhibiting neutrality)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Selection coefficients for three mutants (D87A, D87G, and the triple mutant S83F-D87G-S80I) were slightly negative indicating that these mutants carried fitness costs.
source: while selection coefficients for three mutants (D87A, D87G, and the triple mutant S83F-D87G-S80I) were slightly negative indicating that these mutants carried fitness costs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The largest fitness cost was observed in the triple mutant that demonstrated a 1% reduction in fitness per bacterial generation (MLE s^=−.010).
source: The largest fitness cost was observed in the triple mutant that demonstrated a 1% reduction in fitness per bacterial generation (MLE s^=−.010).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data.

claim: Six mutants had statistically significant positive selection coefficients, ranging from 0.8% to 7.4% per bacterial generation.
source: The remaining six mutants had statistically significant positive selection coefficients, ranging from 0.8% to 7.4% per bacterial generation.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The single mutant with the highest selection coefficient was S83F (MLE s^=+.013).
source: The single mutant with the highest selection coefficient was S83F (MLE s^=+.013)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data.

claim: The double S83F-D87N mutant displayed the highest selection coefficient of all tested strains (MLE s^=+.074).
source: and the double S83F-D87N mutant displayed the highest selection coefficient of all tested strains (MLE s^=+.074).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data.

claim: All of the double mutants demonstrated highly increased fitness over the S. Typhi parent strain and all single mutants.
source: All of the double mutants demonstrated highly increased fitness over the S. Typhi parent strain and all single mutants, suggesting that epistatic interactions among resistance loci may play a role in determining strain fitness.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from competition experiments.

claim: All epistasis parameters (εij) for double mutants were statistically different from zero and positive.
source: Defining fitness for the double mutants as wij = (1 + si) (1 + sj) + εij, we obtained MLEs for the epistasis parameters (εij), all of which were statistically different from zero and positive, indicating that the combined fitness effect of two gyrA mutations (or in one case, a gyrA and a parC mutation) was greater than that predicted under a scenario of multiplicative non-epistasis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The combined fitness effect of two gyrA mutations was greater than that predicted under a scenario of multiplicative non-epistasis.
source: all of which were statistically different from zero and positive, indicating that the combined fitness effect of two gyrA mutations (or in one case, a gyrA and a parC mutation) was greater than that predicted under a scenario of multiplicative non-epistasis (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All three single mutations at codon 87 in the gyrA gene were selectively neutral or nearly-neutral unless in combination with the S83F mutation or the S80I parC mutation.
source: Notably, all three single mutations at codon 87 in the gyrA gene were selectively neutral or nearly-neutral unless in combination with the S83F mutation or the S80I parC mutation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the selection coefficient data.

claim: The S83F and D87N mutations demonstrated the greatest degree of synergistic epistasis, with a 6.6% increase in fitness resulting from the epistatic interaction.
source: The S83F and D87N mutations demonstrated the greatest degree of synergistic epistasis, with a 6.6% increase in fitness resulting from the epistatic interaction.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of epistasis parameters.

claim: The epistasis coefficient for the S83F-D87G-S80I triple mutant relative to the parent strain was negative at −2.6%.
source: We also calculated the epistasis coefficient for the S83F-D87G-S80I triple mutant relative to the parent strain. The epistasis coefficient for this triple mutant was negative at −2.6% (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The interaction between S83F-D87G mutant and the S80I mutation is antagonistic (MLE ε^=−.061).
source: The S83F-D87G mutant has been observed clinically and its interaction with the S80I mutation is antagonistic (MLE ε^=−.061); this is the most likely pathway to the triple mutant.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data.

claim: The interaction between S83F and the laboratory-generated double mutant D87G-S80I is negative (MLE ε^=−.051).
source: The interaction between S83F and the laboratory-generated double mutant D87G-S80I is similarly negative (MLE ε^=−.051).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of competition experiment data.

claim: There is no other bacterial pathogen whose primary routes of drug resistance evolution are associated with such dramatic increases in intrinsic fitness.
source: In conclusion, there is no other bacterial pathogen of which we are currently aware whose primary routes of drug resistance evolution are associated with such dramatic increases in intrinsic fitness.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Fluoroquinolone-resistant strains may be naturally maintained even if the use of this crucial group of antimicrobials is restricted.
source: Our findings have important implications for the selection, maintenance, and treatment of drug-resistant members of the Enterobacteriacea, predicting that fluoroquinolone-resistant strains may be naturally maintained even if the use of this crucial group of antimicrobials is restricted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive fitness coefficients observed.

claim: The attenuated S. Typhi Ty2 strain BRD948 contains deletions in the aroA, aroC and htrA genes.
source: The attenuated S. Typhi Ty2 strain BRD948, containing deletions in the aroA, aroC and htrA genes, was the parent for all bacterial strains (Tacket et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the parent strain used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: S. Typhi BRD948 is auxotrophic for aromatic compounds.
source: S. Typhi BRD948 is a well-characterized laboratory S. Typhi strain, with the attenuating mutations in the aro locus making it auxotrophic for aromatic compounds.
evidence: This is a known property of the strain based on its genetic modifications.

claim: The attenuating mutations in the aro locus affect the ability to grow in the intracellular compartment due to limitation of exogenous aromatic metabolites at this site.
source: These mutations affect the ability to grow in the intracellular compartment due to limitation of exogenous aromatic metabolites at this site.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of attenuation.

claim: The past two decades have seen the emergence of S. Typhi strains exhibiting reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones.
source: The past two decades have seen the emergence of S. Typhi strains exhibiting reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones (Wain et al., 1997; Parry et al., 1998), resulting in the widespread distribution of these strains in almost all locations where typhoid is endemic.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The majority of the epidemic of fluoroquinolone-resistant S. Typhi is associated with one particular genotype (H58).
source: We now know that the majority of this epidemic is associated with one particular genotype (H58), which has swept across Asia and into Africa (Holt et al., 2010; Kariuki et al., 2010; Holt et al., 2011), displacing other genotypes in the process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The H58 genotype has swept across Asia and into Africa, displacing other genotypes in the process.
source: We now know that the majority of this epidemic is associated with one particular genotype (H58), which has swept across Asia and into Africa (Holt et al., 2010; Kariuki et al., 2010; Holt et al., 2011), displacing other genotypes in the process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: There is a strong association between the H58 strains and the S83F gyrA mutation.
source: While this mutation is not unique to this genotype (Roumagnac et al., 2006), there is a strong association between the H58 strains and the S83F gyrA mutation.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological observations supported by citation.

claim: There is a strong correlation between reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and prolonged infection.
source: There are currently no data directly comparing S. Typhi genotype and disease outcome in typhoid patients; there is, however, a strong correlation between reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones (caused by the S83F mutation) and prolonged infection (Parry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: The dominance of the H58 genotype may not stem solely from therapeutic fluoroquinolone usage.
source: Our data suggest that the dominance of the H58 genotype, the current global clonal expansion, and the emergence of other strains with reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones may not stem solely from therapeutic fluoroquinolone usage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive fitness coefficients observed in the absence of antimicrobials.

claim: Positive selection of bacteria with gyrA mutations has been predicted by mechanisms inducing DNA supercoiling continuation via suboptimal topoisomerases and modifications that enhance the functionality of the gyrA promoter.
source: Indeed, positive selection of bacteria with gyrA mutations has been predicted by mechanisms inducing DNA supercoiling continuation via suboptimal topoisomerases and modifications that enhance the functionality of the gyrA promoter (Marcusson et al., 2009; Balsalobre et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mechanistic studies.

claim: An antimicrobial control strategy, including the withdrawal of fluoroquinolones from general usage within the population, is unlikely to reduce the population-level frequencies of antimicrobial resistance to these drugs.
source: As the majority of S. Typhi strains described here do not exhibit a fitness cost, an antimicrobial control strategy, including the withdrawal of fluoroquinolones from general usage within the population, is unlikely to reduce the population-level frequencies of antimicrobial resistance to these drugs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive fitness coefficients observed.

claim: There would be a continued rise in the frequency of fluoroquinolone-resistance, even in the absence of sustained drug exposure.
source: In fact, our results indicate that there would be a continued rise in the frequency of fluoroquinolone-resistance, even in the absence of sustained drug exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive fitness coefficients observed.

claim: Competing genetically unrelated clinical isolates may make it difficult to isolate the effects of a single mutation.
source: Competing genetically unrelated clinical isolates (Laurent et al., 2001; Wichelhaus et al., 2002), or strains that are otherwise imperfectly isogenic, may make it difficult to isolate the effects of a single mutation (Enne et al., 2005; Komp Lindgren et al., 2005; Gagneux et al., 2006; MacLean and Buckling, 2009; O'Regan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Bacterial enumeration and selective culturing after serial dilutions can be affected by experimental variation or spontaneous mutations.
source: Furthermore, bacterial enumeration and selective culturing after serial dilutions are typically used to calculate population sizes (Laurent et al., 2001; Wichelhaus et al., 2002; Macvanin et al., 2003; Gagneux et al., 2006; Rozen et al., 2007; Balsalobre and de la Campa, 2008; MacLean and Buckling, 2009; Randall et al., 2008), and these methodologies can be affected by experimental variation or spontaneous mutations in the target gene(s) as a consequence of exposure to low levels of antimicrobial.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: S. Typhi is a human-restricted facultative intracellular organism.
source: S. Typhi is a human-restricted facultative intracellular organism, and the selection coefficients that we observed using an S. Typhi aro mutant strain in an in vitro media-derived competitive growth assay system may not be replicated in other experimental systems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. Typhi biology.

claim: There is currently no in vivo or in vitro experimental system outside humans or primates that accurately mimics an S. Typhi infection cycle.
source: However, there is currently no in vivo or in vitro experimental system outside humans or primates that accurately mimics an S. Typhi infection cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current experimental models.

claim: S. Typhi invades intestinal epithelial cells (M cells) and uses the macrophage as a vehicle for systemic dissemination.
source: S. Typhi invades intestinal epithelial cells (M cells) and uses the macrophage as a vehicle for systemic dissemination
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. Typhi pathogenesis.

claim: Individuals that carry S. Typhi asymptomatically in their gallbladder are thought to play an important role in the maintenance and dissemination of S. Typhi strains.
source: For example, individuals that carry S. Typhi asymptomatically in their gallbladder are thought to play an important role in the maintenance and dissemination of S. Typhi strains (Dongol et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: S. Typhi is hypothesized to replicate extracellularly in the gallbladder.
source: and S. Typhi is hypothesized to replicate extracellularly in the gallbladder (Gonzalez-Escobedo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The positive selection coefficients measured for gyrA/parC mutations are consistent with the current understanding of the microbiology and molecular epidemiology of S. Typhi.
source: Notwithstanding these experimental limitations, the positive selection coefficients we measure for our gyrA and parC mutations are consistent with the current understanding of the microbiology and molecular epidemiology of S. Typhi.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental results to broader epidemiological patterns.

claim: The S83F mutation is not unique to the H58 genotype.
source: While this mutation is not unique to this genotype (Roumagnac et al., 2006), there is a strong association between the H58 strains and the S83F gyrA mutation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous phylogenetic research.

claim: The S83F mutation provides the most probable primary foundation for the evolution of fluoroquinolone-resistant S. Typhi.
source: Of these two mutations, it is S83F that exhibits both the greatest selection coefficient and the highest MIC to the fluoroquinolones, making the emergence or establishment of S80I variants evolutionary less likely. The S83F mutation provides the most probable primary foundation for the evolution of fluoroquinolone-resistant S. Typhi.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fitness and MIC data.

claim: The S83F mutation has arisen on multiple occasions in several lineages.
source: Phylogenetic investigations have shown that the S83F mutation has arisen on multiple occasions in several lineages (Roumagnac et al., 2006; Holt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The ability of S83F mutants to catalyze positive epistatic interactions with other otherwise neutral mutations suggests that new S83F combinations may be observed more frequently in the future.
source: Additionally, the ability of S83F mutants to catalyze positive epistatic interactions with other otherwise neutral mutations suggests that new S83F combinations may be observed more frequently in the future (Koirala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the epistasis data.

claim: Typhoid is a disease that necessitates antimicrobial therapy.
source: Typhoid is a disease that necessitates antimicrobial therapy and the results presented here have repercussions for typhoid therapy and control.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: The control of typhoid across Asia and Africa relies on fluoroquinolone treatment.
source: Currently, the control of typhoid across Asia and Africa relies on fluoroquinolone treatment (WHO, 2003), often prescribed in endemic settings for any non-specific low-grade febrile disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: Many locations are observing a preponderance of strains that have elevated MICs to fluoroquinolones.
source: However, many locations are observing a preponderance of strains that have elevated MICs to fluoroquinolones, resulting from the gyrA and parC mutations we have assessed here (Holt et al., 2010; Kariuki et al., 2010; Holt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous epidemiological studies.

claim: Incremental increases in MICs to fluoroquinolones correspond directly with treatment failure and disease severity.
source: These observations are of great concern as incremental increases in MICs to fluoroquinolones correspond directly with treatment failure and disease severity (Parry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical research.

claim: Antimicrobial resistance and an inability to clear infection may have obvious consequences for prolonged asymptomatic carriage of these pathogens.
source: Furthermore, antimicrobial resistance and an inability to clear infection may have obvious consequences for prolonged asymptomatic carriage of these pathogens.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the public health implications.
